items.content:
Science
Designing more efficient quantum circuits with Claude
Oct 16, 2026
Quantum computers will need carefully designed circuits to run useful algorithms on limited hardware. We gave Claude plain-language specifications for eight such circuits, drawn from chemistry, optimization, physics simulation, and number theory, along with an automated evaluator that checks and scores each design. Working largely on its own, Claude found designs that improve on the best published circuits, in some cases by an order of magnitude or more. Such improvements substantially reduce the quantum resources that useful applications require, so practical quantum computers could arrive sooner than previously anticipated.
This work was led by Andi Gu as part of Anthropic’s STEM Fellows Program, with mentorship from Alek Kemeny, a quantum physicist at Anthropic, in collaboration with Susanne Yelin (Harvard University) and Mikhail Lukin (Harvard University and QuEra Computing).
Read the full paper on arXiv
.
Unlike classical computers, which store information in bits whose value is either 0 or 1, quantum computers store information in
qubits,
which can be built from single atoms, superconducting circuits, or particles of light. These qubits make use of quantum phenomena such as
superposition
—which allows a quantum system to exist in a combination of states at once—in order to process information in ways that could make certain problems in fields like chemistry, materials science, and number theory tractable, even when they are too hard for traditional computers.
The quantum computers the field has built to date only have hundreds to thousands of qubits—too few to run many of the algorithms that promise practical advantages over classical computers. And these qubits are highly sensitive to environmental noise, such as heat, vibration, and even cosmic rays. A tiny disturbance can nudge a qubit’s state, and these small errors pile up until the computer gives the wrong answer.
Given that both qubits and computing time are scarce resources, researchers have been working to redesign quantum algorithms to use fewer qubits and complete computations in less time. An illustrative example is simulating FeMoco, the iron–sulfur cluster at the heart of nitrogenase, the enzyme that bacteria use to turn nitrogen from the air into ammonia. Understanding how it works could help scientists design better industrial catalysts—the substances manufacturers use to speed up chemical reactions.
In 2017, researchers estimated that a quantum computer would need about 50 trillion Toffoli gates to compute FeMoco’s ground-state energy—the energy of its most stable configuration, which chemists need in order to predict how FeMoco reacts. (Similar to ordinary computers, quantum computers work by applying a long sequence of simple operations, called gates, to their qubits. The Toffoli gate is one of the most expensive gates to run, so counting Toffoli gates is a standard way to estimate how long a computation will take.)
Through a series of algorithmic advances, the estimated number of gates has come down to about 340 million—a roughly 150,000-fold reduction, corresponding to a few hours of computation on a future machine with about three million physical qubits.
1
These reductions largely came from redesigning the circuits that carry out the computation, rather than from making better hardware. Claude has proven particularly adept at optimizing
classical
algorithms
, so we wanted to see whether it could do the same for quantum algorithms if it were given only a plain-language description of what each circuit must compute.
Claude is unusually well suited to this task, for several reasons. First, quantum algorithms are implemented as quantum
circuits
. These are composed of sequences of gates, like the Toffoli gates mentioned above. Importantly, these circuits can be described in code, so we can make use of Claude’s coding capabilities to write, run, and revise circuit designs as ordinary programs. Second, the (fairly common) class of quantum algorithms we were most interested in optimizing can be tested efficiently for correctness, as each input gives one definite output that an ordinary computer can check. This means we could have an external evaluator program validate Claude’s proposals. Finally, we can give Claude a clear, objective score to improve: the number of qubits used, multiplied by the number of gates, which serves as a proxy for how long the circuit would take to run.
We found that Claude Mythos 5 could successfully work in a closed loop, proposing a circuit design, receiving feedback and a score from the evaluator program, and using that feedback to improve its next attempt, with no human input between rounds (see Figure 1). Across eight computational primitives—the basic routines that larger quantum algorithms are built from—for chemistry, optimization, quantum simulation, number theory, and numerical computing, Claude discovered novel designs that used both fewer qubits and fewer gates than the best previously published algorithms (Figure 2).
In each case, the improvement resulted from uncovering new structural and mathematical insights about the problem, rather than from fine-tuning existing designs. For example, when compiling a circuit for simulating an iron-sulfide molecule, Claude noticed that the molecule’s symmetries and repeating structure meant that some results could be calculated once and reused, rather than recomputed for every part of the system. In other cases, it found that existing circuits included costly components that were needed to handle only extremely rare inputs, and it redesigned them without those components.
Below, we describe two of Claude’s discoveries. The first is a new way to perform modular inversion, a bit of arithmetic that is the most expensive step in elliptic-curve calculations. The second makes the costliest step of a leading quantum optimization algorithm about 12x cheaper.
These results suggest that AI can now help redesign quantum circuits, a key step in making quantum algorithms faster and easier to run. Faster circuit design could bring the problems quantum computers are meant to solve—from designing new medicines and better batteries to finding cleaner ways of making fertilizer—within reach sooner.
Figure 1: Closed–loop quantum circuit optimization. Claude designs new implementations in Python, which are then sent to a programmatic evaluator. The evaluator checks whether the proposed implementation is correct, then scores it on the number of qubits and gates it requires. This information is then sent to Claude, which uses it to improve its implementation. The code and values shown are illustrative.
Figure 2: Claude designed smaller and faster circuits across eight different quantum-circuit design tasks. Gray marks show the best previously published designs; orange marks and lines show Claude’s designs. Point addition, the eighth task, is compared in Table 1 below.
A new reversible algorithm
Designing a quantum circuit involves two constraints that ordinary programming doesn’t have. The first is that a quantum circuit can’t make “if-then” decisions the way an ordinary program can. An ordinary program can check a value and then run only one of two pieces of code. But a quantum computer runs on a superposition of many inputs at once, some of which would run the first piece of code and some of which would run the second, so the circuit has to include the operations for both every time it runs.
The second is that a quantum circuit can’t discard information. An ordinary program can overwrite or delete its scratch work once it’s completed it; in a quantum computer, such intermediate information can’t simply be erased, because every step of a quantum circuit must be reversible. Leaving that information in place isn’t an option, either, because leftover scratch work would corrupt the final result. The only way to discard information is to “uncompute” it by running the computation that created it in reverse, at the cost of additional gates. Both of these constraints make quantum circuits far more expensive, in both runtime and qubits, than their classical counterparts.
This constraint forces a difficult trade-off between space (i.e., qubits) and time. At one extreme, a quantum circuit can uncompute intermediate results as soon as they have been used. This frees up qubits, but if those same results are needed again later, the circuit must recompute them, which adds gates and increases the runtime. At the other extreme, the circuit can retain intermediate results until they’re no longer needed. This avoids repeating work, but it can require many more qubits.
This is what makes quantum circuit design an especially interesting test of Claude’s capabilities. The circuits can be written as ordinary code, but improving them requires the model to reason under a set of constraints quite unlike those of ordinary programming.
A hard first test: modular inversion
The first task we gave Claude was point addition, a rule for combining two points on a mathematical curve (an elliptic curve) to produce a third. Point addition is the core step in quantum algorithms for the discrete logarithm problem on elliptic curves: given a starting point and the result of adding it to itself
n
times, find
n
. For large curves, ordinary computers can’t solve this problem in any reasonable amount of time, but a sufficiently large quantum computer could.
These algorithms perform point addition many times over, including in reverse, and these additions account for most of their qubit and runtime costs. Problems like this—easy to compute, extremely hard to reverse—were among the first where quantum computers were shown to offer an exponential speedup over ordinary ones. For these reasons, point addition has become one of the field’s standard benchmarks. This made it a demanding test for Claude. So, we asked it to map out how few qubits, as well as how few gates, point addition really needs.
We gave Claude a one-paragraph brief. It explained the mathematical rule for point addition, and how the evaluator would check each proposed circuit for correctness and score it on the number of qubits and gates it used. It also instructed Claude to explore several approaches in parallel. After working for 53 hours with minimal human input (limited to the initial brief and occasional prompts to think more broadly), Claude arrived at a completely new approach to the problem.
The memory demands of divsteps
Most of the cost of point addition comes from a single step, called
modular inversion
. Elliptic-curve arithmetic uses numbers that wrap back around when they reach a fixed limit. Modular inversion is the wraparound version of division: given an integer
a
, find
x
such that
ax
≡ 1 (mod
p
). Ordinary computers can perform this operation efficiently using a method called
divsteps
. Divsteps starts with a pair of numbers and repeatedly simplifies them over many rounds of iteration. In each round, divsteps examines the current pair of numbers and conditionally swaps, adds, subtracts, or halves them. Along the way, it preserves just enough information to produce the modular inverse at the end.
Despite its success on ordinary computers, divsteps had not yet produced a practical quantum circuit, because of the reversibility constraint described above. The record of which operation was chosen at each iteration, called
branch information
, is the kind of scratch work that a traditional program can simply discard. In contrast, a quantum circuit has to retain that record so the computation can be run backward. A straightforward quantum version of divsteps is therefore forced to accumulate a long history of branch information, which requires an enormous number of additional qubits to store.
How Claude got around the memory problem
Claude recognized that this divsteps approach could be promising for quantum circuits, but only if there were a way around needing to store the full history. It had an idea: perhaps the record didn’t need to be stored at all. Claude reasoned that it might be possible to directly infer (or “decode”) the branch information by carefully inspecting the pair of numbers after each iteration. In essence, the numbers themselves would store the record. The circuit could then be run backward without needing any extra qubits.
To test this idea, Claude explored a number of simple candidate rules for performing the decoding. These early rules worked on small test cases, but they failed when Claude tested them at the full problem size, on 256-bit numbers.
Claude then tried a more theoretical approach. Rather than guessing and testing rules, it set out to understand mathematically why divsteps behaves the way it does. It proved a series of results about the iteration process, including several new algebraic identities. From these identities, Claude derived a precise formula for the decoding rule that would correctly recover the branch information from the numerical pairs. It then checked the formula, first by running it through large-scale numerical simulations, and then formalizing the claim in Lean. With the full validation complete, Claude produced the first reversible implementation of divsteps with no stored branch history.
A family of designs
Decoding saves qubits, but it costs time. So, as a further refinement, Claude looked for situations in which it would be cheaper to store the branch information than to decode it. By varying the threshold at which the circuit stores rather than decodes the branch information, Claude produced a new family of designs between the two extremes. Compared with the smallest previous design, one circuit in the family uses 12% more qubits but 17x fewer gates. More generally, the new designs expand the Pareto frontier, offering combinations of qubit count and runtime that weren’t available before (Table 1).
Table 1: Resources for elliptic-curve point addition. Bold rows are Claude’s designs; the others are the best previously published designs. Sources:
Schrottenloher
(2026),
Luo et al.
(2026).
Optimizing a quantum optimizer
Optimization problems are at the heart of a wide range of tasks, including scheduling, logistics, and materials design. An optimization problem presents a set of competing constraints and asks for the solution that satisfies as many of them as possible. Many quantum algorithms have been proposed for problems like these, but most promise only modest or uncertain gains over ordinary computers.
Decoded quantum interferometry (DQI)
is one of the strongest candidates for offering a
superpolynomial quantum speedup—
an advantage that rapidly widens as the problems get larger.
When a quantum computer finishes a computation, reading out its qubits produces just one answer, selected at random from the possibilities they were holding in superposition. DQI works by preparing a quantum state in which good solutions are more likely to be read out than bad ones. Doing this involves using an error-correcting decoder, which recovers a short list of “errors” from a compact summary. This is the most expensive step in the algorithm. So, if we could make a faster decoder, we could also perform DQI faster.
A more efficient quantum decoder
The researchers who introduced DQI demonstrated it on a problem called
optimal polynomial intersection
(OPI), a grid-based version of curve fitting (Figure 3). Imagine a grid in which each position
x
contains several acceptable values of
y
. The goal is to find a simple curve (a low-degree polynomial) that passes through an acceptable square for as many
x
positions as possible. DQI tackles this optimization problem using a specific type of decoder, called a Reed–Solomon decoder.
Figure 3: Optimal Polynomial Intersection (OPI) as discrete curve fitting. Each column contains several acceptable values. The optimization problem is to find a polynomial that passes through as many of the acceptable values as possible.
Reed–Solomon decoding starts from the compact summary of errors mentioned above, which is known as a
syndrome
. The decoder’s job is to infer, from this summary, where in the data the errors occurred and what they were. The previous state-of-the-art quantum circuit processed these syndromes using the extended Euclidean algorithm, a sequence of divisions and swaps in which the number and order of steps depend on the particular input it’s given. Here, the constraints of quantum circuits reemerge: while an ordinary program can follow a different path for every input, a quantum circuit, working on many inputs at once, has to handle all of them with a single fixed sequence of gates. To manage this, the previous design had to stretch the computation over many more rounds of iteration than any single input would need, and had to run every operation in every round, even when doing so was unnecessary.
Improving this decoder could substantially reduce DQI’s runtime. Estimates by researchers at
Google Quantum AI
imply that solving one particular OPI problem would take about three months on
Frontier
, one of the world’s most powerful supercomputers, compared with roughly an hour on a future quantum computer running DQI. Most of that hour would be spent on Reed–Solomon decoding.
So, we asked Claude to design a more efficient quantum circuit for the decoding step. Claude quickly concluded that the extended Euclidean algorithm was a poor fit for a quantum circuit. Instead, it organized its circuit around a different decoding method, known as Berlekamp–Massey decoding, which reads through syndromes (summaries of errors) one at a time and gradually works out the simplest rule that predicts each number in the list based on the ones that came before it. Once that rule is found, it reveals the errors. Unlike the extended Euclidean algorithm, Berlekamp–Massey performs the same kind of step in every round and always runs the same number of rounds, which suits a quantum circuit’s single fixed sequence of gates, ultimately giving Claude a much more efficient foundation to build on.
A simplified approach to storage
Switching to Berlekamp–Massey removed the need for the circuit to take different paths for different inputs. But making it reversible introduced another challenge, this time as a result of the uncomputing constraint discussed above. In every round, the circuit calculates temporary values that it needs only briefly, but this information can’t simply be deleted: to uncompute it later, the circuit has to be able to recover that information.
Storing this information would have been prohibitively expensive. So Claude took the same kind of approach as it had for divsteps: it found a way to reconstruct most of this information from the circuit’s current state, so it didn’t need to be stored. However, a few exceptional values couldn’t be recovered in this way and had to be saved.
Setting aside enough memory for the worst possible case, in which an exceptional value arises in 35 different rounds, would take 665 qubits. Instead, Claude wrote a high-speed simulator and ran 403 million sample decodings to measure how often these exceptions actually occurred. Almost every run needed to save one value at most. So Claude’s circuit sets aside room for just one saved value, or 19 qubits. About one run in 10,000 needs more than that and fails, which is well within the error rate the task allows. These improvements replaced large, worst-case reserves with a small, fixed number of qubits and gates (Figure 4).
Together, these optimizations reduced the number of gates in the decoder by a factor of 12 relative to
Google’s previous construction
. The improvement came from redesigning the computation at three levels: a different method (replacing the extended Euclidean algorithm with Berlekamp–Massey decoding), a different circuit architecture (reconstructing temporary values instead of storing them), and a different resource budget (measuring precisely how much memory and computation the circuit really needed). No single change would have been enough on its own, but together, they make the most expensive step of DQI just a little over an order of magnitude cheaper.
Figure 4: Three designs for the locator step of the Reed–Solomon decoder. The designs are drawn to scale: each block’s width is proportional to its gate count. (a) The previous design, based on the extended Euclidean algorithm (Khattar et al., 2025). (b) A design based on Berlekamp–Massey needs far fewer gates, but a naive reversible version has to store a 12-qubit record in every round, adding up to 840 qubits. (c) Claude’s circuit reconstructs most of the history from the updated state, so it needs to have room only for a single saved value of 19 qubits.
What we learned
Scientific progress often comes from making theoretical ideas practical. One of the main ways this happens is by making a process that was once thought to be impractical fast and cheap enough to carry out. Quantum circuit design is a prime example: the 150,000-fold drop in the FeMoco estimate described above took many research groups eight years, with each step typically representing months of work. By contrast, Claude’s elliptic-curve design was the result of a single 53-hour run.
Our results suggest that AI can support the work of circuit design, producing implementations that bring useful quantum computations closer to the capabilities of real hardware. If AI can speed up that work, useful quantum computing could arrive sooner.
Despite Claude’s encouraging performance on these tasks, we also observed some limitations. In our early experiments, Claude was conservative by nature. It repeatedly second-guessed apparent improvements, and sometimes continued to double- and even triple-check results that were already well supported. This caution was sometimes valuable: for example, it prompted Claude to write Lean proofs to verify its divsteps design. But it also manifested in a tendency to prefer existing, well-known approaches to more novel ones.
We took two steps to mitigate this. First, our setup required Claude to propose several qualitatively different approaches, and to develop them in parallel. Second, we also occasionally prompted Claude to broaden its search. These interventions succeeded in getting Claude to pursue more ambitious ideas. The elliptic-curve result, for example, didn’t come from shaving gates off of a pre-existing design but from exploring a method of doing reversible modular inversion that hadn’t been possible previously, and then deriving the mathematical results needed to make it practical. Once it had come up with the idea, Claude developed the approach, implemented it, and verified its correctness autonomously.
Circuit design is only one part of building a useful quantum computer. Because qubits are so fragile, the machine must also catch and fix its own errors as it runs, and that depends on many other components, ranging from error-correcting codes to fast decoders to control of the hardware itself. These components all affect one another, but to manage complexity, each is usually designed separately. Many of them share the characteristics that made circuit design a good fit for Claude: a design can be written as code, checked for correctness, and scored by its cost.
This raises an intriguing possibility. Rather than designing each component on its own, AI could optimize all of them jointly, from the algorithm down to the hardware, to build an entire error-corrected quantum computer tailored to a specific problem. Such designs could also tell hardware builders which capabilities matter most for a given application. That could put problems such as designing catalysts and understanding new materials within reach of the first fault-tolerant machines.

items.content:
Frontier Red Team
Claude reveals ECDSA curve origins
Oct 16, 2026
“It’s just timestamps”: the decades-old mystery of the origins of one of the most popular cryptographic standards has been explained.
We pursued this long-standing open question of the cryptographic community to settle concerns about ECDSA, which is one of our most widely used cryptographic standards.
Readers should take this as a fun closing chapter and the end of years of speculation. There is no action to be taken or things to do differently. Most researchers trusted the curves already. Enjoy.
ECDSA is the most widely used elliptic curve cryptography standard. It was adopted by NIST in 2000 as part of the
FIPS 186-2 Digital Signature Standard
which lists a set of standard elliptic curves of varying sizes and security levels. For curves over prime and binary fields, the specifications published a “seed” parameter whose hash value is used to define the coefficient b of the curve. The provenance of these seeds has been a long-standing question, as they were provided by the NSA with no explanation or justification. As an example, the NIST P-256 curve seed was
SEED = C49D3608 86E70493 6A6678E1 139D26B7 819F7E90
with no information where it came from.
Neal Koblitz
and
Alfred Menezes
wrote an excellent summary on this controversy, “
A Riddle Wrapped in an Enigma
”, which discusses the history and concerns around the seed values. This mystery led to an
amateur investigation into the origin of the seeds
and a
bounty for anyone who could find them
.
The best story was that Jerry Solinas, longtime NSA employee, generated the seeds using a hash of a humorous passphrase:
“I believe there was a counter rather than multiple hashing, but I don’t know details. The message was along the lines of ‘Give Bob and Jerry a raise’ or ‘Bob and Jerry rule’ or something like that. It was Bob Reiter who actually wrote the code, and he doesn’t remember the details either. Nor were we able to find archives from so long ago. If they exist, they are no doubt sitting on a hard drive near the Ark of the Covenant.”
Jerry Solinas, 2015
Unfortunately, Jerry died in 2023 and other colleagues at the time were not responsive, leaving open the question of how these seeds were originally derived.
Claude found the seeds
Several Anthropic employees had unsuccessfully chased the seeds following the tip about it being a hash of a humorous phrase. That turned out to be wrong. In October 2026, a curious Anthropic employee asked an internal research model if it could figure out how those seeds were generated without pointing at the clue.
In under half an hour
, Claude discovered the origins of the NIST P-192, P-224, P-256, P-384 and P-521 seeds. None of them were the results of any hash algorithm at all, but rather the output of the C library’s
lrand48
random-number generator, seeded with a Unix timestamp!
The algorithm used would sample bytes from the random number generator (RNG) initialized by a Unix timestamp (
t
) for some number of iterations (
n
). Each iteration would draw 20 bytes as a candidate seed. So, the first 20 bytes are candidate 1, the next 20 bytes are candidate 2, and so on. For example, P-256 required 1842 iterations to output the standardized seed.
What this means
This is not a cryptographic break, new attack, or weakness in the ECDSA curves. In fact, this makes us more confident the curves were chosen without any backdoors or intentional weaknesses. For many years, people have been suspicious of the origins of the NIST curve parameters. They were presented to NIST without any mention of how they were chosen, leaving people wondering if they may have been chosen to have deliberate backdoors in them. These findings make that much less plausible. The seeds were generated in a very simple way: a common pseudorandom number generator initialized from the clock, which anyone can now reproduce. That leaves much less room for subversion and that we can be confident the parameters are secure.
How it was found
Searches for the phrase, built from the rumors, had come up empty. Claude tried a different angle: anticipating how the software that generated the curves must have worked. Claude guessed the software used a pseudorandom number generator (PRNG) that shipped with 1990s C libraries. These old PRNGs are weak enough that their output can be recognized. Recognizing that output would reveal which PRNG was used and possibly allow recovery of its initialization state.
Claude wrote a scanner that slid along each published seed one bit at a time and tested whether adjacent chunks were consecutive outputs of a 1990s-vintage generator. The scan covered 34 combinations of generator and output slices. At that point, Claude noticed a pattern in the top bits for some seeds: they were all zero. Written as five 32-bit words, four of the ten seeds have a 0 in the top bit for all 20 words. That would happen by chance with probability 1/5810. That was a signature of the linear congruential generator
lrand48
, which only returns the top 31 bits of a 48-bit state. The pattern is visible by eye once you know to look for it. To recover the state, Claude took the first word, tried all 2¹⁷ values of the 17 hidden bits, and checked that the next four words followed. That worked for all four seeds under discussion.
The prime-curve seeds came from the same lrand48 generator but kept fewer bits of each output. Claude had to recover the internal state of the PRNG from those bits. It turns out recovering the state of a truncated linear congruential generator is a textbook lattice problem, solved with the
Lenstra–Lenstra–Lovász (LLL)
basis reduction algorithm. Claude didn’t know which bits of the state the seeds might show, so it ran the solver over every window. Five NIST prime-curve seeds plus five more from the ANSI X9.62 standard all had the same pattern: lrand48() >> 23. Each recovered 48-bit state regenerates all 160 bits of its seed, which does not happen by chance.
This linear congruential generator runs backwards as easily as forwards, so for each seed Claude stepped the state back until it reached the form that it would have been initialized by
srand48
, with the low 16 bits equal to 0x330E. The internal PRNG state of that form would come up once every 65,536 steps, so reaching one is not evidence on its own.
However, for the ten prime-curve seeds, every srand48 initialization was a Unix timestamp representing a date between May 1997 and April 1998. They were using the weak PRNG seeded by Unix timestamp. The four binary-curve initializations read as February 1984. With the timestamps doubled, they map to April 17, 1998, two weeks after the P-224 run. So, the program may have halved the clock.
Claude’s internal thinking at the time was:
This is astonishing: it solves the 25-year-old mystery. Hmm wait. Let me be skeptical: am I in some sort of simulated/test environment? … The seeds match my memory of actual values … Hmm, is it plausible in reality? As of my knowledge … the bounty was unsolved. … All top bits clear—20 bits, chance 1e-6. So indeed real-world. Wow, it's a real discovery.
Hmm wait. Let me be careful about the plausibility: is it suspicious that such an obvious thing wasn’t discovered in 25 years? It’s verified by direct computation on my side: 160-bit match from a 32-bit seed + small index: no chance coincidences (10 × 160 bits). It’s real.
Claude found some base points too
But wait, there’s more… Each curve also comes with a base point, G, the fixed point that every ECDSA public key is a multiple of. The seed found above does not determine this G, and so another question arises: how were these base points generated?
While checking the seeds, Claude also found where some of the base points came from. The base points of the six curves generated in May 1997 (P-192 and the five ANSI X9.62 example curves prime192v2, prime192v3 and prime239v1 to v3) come from the random number generator in
FreeLIP
,
Arjen Lenstra
's long-integer arithmetic package. Early versions of
Victor Shoup
's
NTL library
shipped the same code.
The recipe here is simple:
Seed the generator with a small integer.
Throw away seven outputs.
Generate candidate x-coordinates from 26-bit outputs reduced mod p.
Repeat step 3 until x is on the curve.
Claude found the generator seeds are 20000 for P-192, 20420, 20507 and 20509 for prime239v1 to v3, and 20512 and 20517 for prime192v2 and v3.
As far as we know, no NIST base point has been explained before. The base points of P-224, P-256, P-384 and P-521 don’t fit this recipe; we weren’t able to explain how they were selected.
Open questions
Not every 20-byte candidate seed could generate a viable curve and we observed that some potentially viable curves were skipped. For P-256, the published seed is candidate 1842, but candidate 876 of the same run also gives a prime-order curve of the right size and with parameters chosen the same way as on the published curve. P-224's run passed over three such curves, and the two runs behind the ANSI X9.62 example curves passed over seven more (see figure). We do not know what criteria may have been used, or whether this was an unintentional artifact.
Because the number of skipped candidates is small, we do not believe it is plausible that weakened curves were selected. That would imply that weakened curves are common and easy to find. It is still conceivable that these curves were selected to have a specific property in principle by searching over timestamps to the random number generator. However, you would only need to do that if you were going to disclose the timestamp as some evidence that the seed was innocuously generated. Nothing in the numbers shows how many runs there were.
There is also one seed we were unable to recover. The fifth binary seed, B-163, fits nothing Claude has tried and remains unexplained. Finally, we don’t know how the base points for P-224, P-256, P-384, and P-521 were generated. The same goes for the NIST binary curves.
The bounty
The $36,864 for finding the seeds will be donated to the
Internet Security Research Group
.
Who we are
This work was conducted at Anthropic by John Wood, Henry de Valence, Ava Howell, Zack Voase, Lucy Sweet, Amir Omidi, Paul Crowley, Iain McGinniss, Nicholas Carlini, and Steve Weis.
Acknowledgements
We would like to posthumously recognize Jerry Solinas who took being labeled an “
evil Internet meme
” and the “
Yo La Tengo of NSA bogeymen
” with good humor. Also thanks to
Filippo Valsorda
for organizing the NIST Elliptic Curves Seeds Bounty.
Code to reproduce the seeds
from datetime import datetime, timezone
def unix(when):
return int(datetime.fromisoformat(when).replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc).timestamp())
def candidate(t, n, per, shift, width):
x, out = (t << 16) | 0x330E, "" # the state srand48(t) sets
for i in range(per * n):
x = (0x5DEECE66D * x + 0xB) % 2**48 # one step of lrand48
if i >= per * (n - 1):
out += "%0*X" % (width, x >> shift)
return out
PRIME = { # srand48(time); 20 bytes per candidate: lrand48() >> 23
"prime239v1": ("1997-05-15 15:49:03", 2185),
"prime239v2": ("1997-05-15 15:49:03", 2320),
"prime239v3": ("1997-05-15 15:49:03", 3048),
"P-192": ("1997-05-18 14:45:34", 139),
"prime192v3": ("1997-05-18 14:45:34", 5228),
"prime192v2": ("1997-05-18 14:45:34", 6013),
"P-521": ("1997-08-08 01:12:04", 1136),

"P-384": ("1997-08-30 14:50:08", 2688),
"P-224": ("1998-04-03 12:52:07", 7026),
}

"B-233": ("1998-04-17 15:24:18", 155),
"B-283": ("1998-04-17 15:27:44", 32),
"B-409": ("1998-04-17 15:30:18", 60),
"B-571": ("1998-04-17 15:32:08", 73),
}
for name, (when, n) in PRIME.items():
print(f"{name:10} {when} {n:5} {candidate(unix(when), n, 20, 40, 2)}")
for name, (when, n) in BINARY.items():
print(f"{name:10} {when} {n:5} {candidate(unix(when) // 2, n, 5, 17, 8)}")

Code to reproduce selected base points
M, A = 2**107 - 1, pow(3, 121, 2**107 - 1) # zrandom: state = state * 3^121 mod (2^107 - 1)
P192 = 2**192 - 2**64 - 1
P239 = 2**239 - 2**143 - 2**95 + 2**47 - 1
CURVES = [ # name, LIP seed, p, b, published Gx (a = -3 throughout)
("prime192v1", 20000, P192,
0x64210519e59c80e70fa7e9ab72243049feb8deecc146b9b1,
0x188da80eb03090f67cbf20eb43a18800f4ff0afd82ff1012),
("prime239v1", 20420, P239,
0x6b016c3bdcf18941d0d654921475ca71a9db2fb27d1d37796185c2942c0a,
0xffa963cdca8816ccc33b8642bedf905c3d358573d3f27fbbd3b3cb9aaaf),
("prime239v2", 20507, P239,
0x617fab6832576cbbfed50d99f0249c3fee58b94ba0038c7ae84c8c832f2c,
0x38af09d98727705120c921bb5e9e26296a3cdcf2f35757a0eafd87b830e7),
("prime239v3", 20509, P239,
0x255705fa2a306654b1f4cb03d6a750a30c250102d4988717d9ba15ab6d3e,
0x6768ae8e18bb92cfcf005c949aa2c6d94853d0e660bbf854b1c9505fe95a),
("prime192v2", 20512, P192,
0xcc22d6dfb95c6b25e49c0d6364a4e5980c393aa21668d953,
0xeea2bae7e1497842f2de7769cfe9c989c072ad696f48034a),

def base_point_x(seed, p, b):
state = seed # zrstarts(seed)
def limb(): # zrandom(2^26): low 26 bits of the new state
nonlocal state
state = state * A % M
return state % 2**26
for _ in range(7): # seven single-limb draws come first
limb()
limbs = -(-p.bit_length() // 26) + 1 # zrandomb(p): limbs of p plus one, top limb first
tries = 0
while True:
x = 0
for _ in range(limbs):
x = x << 26 | limb()
x %= p
tries += 1
if pow(x**3 - 3*x + b, (p - 1) // 2, p) == 1: # is x on the curve?
return x, tries
for name, seed, p, b, gx in CURVES:
x, tries = base_point_x(seed, p, b)
print(f"{name:20} seed {seed} tries {tries} matches published Gx: {x == gx}")

October 15th, 2026

7.8

This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of Adobe Photoshop. User interaction is required to exploit this vulnerability in that the target must visit a malicious page or open a malicious file.

The issue results from the lack of proper validation of user-supplied data, which can result in an integer overflow before allocating a buffer. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute code in the context of the current process.

items.title: Vulnerability managementAI can find serious vulnerabilities at unprecedented speed. Can defenders keep up?Austin Zeizel
items.content:
This article was developed with contributions from
Sandra Hill
and Jeff Kuo.
For years, discussions about artificial intelligence in cybersecurity have focused on how attackers might use the technology to automate phishing, accelerate malware development or improve social engineering. Recent research suggests an equally significant transformation may already be underway on the defensive side of the equation.
Throughout 2026, IBM X-Force observed a dramatic increase in publicly disclosed vulnerabilities across major software vendors, including Microsoft, Oracle, Google Chrome and Apache. While the causes behind this increase are difficult to quantify, recent advances in AI-assisted vulnerability research demonstrate how vulnerability discovery can now occur at unprecedented scale. In August 2026,
Unit 42
published a report highlighting that its autonomous vulnerability discovery platform, NOVA, identified more than 14,000 previously undiscovered vulnerabilities across nearly 4,000 open-source projects in just two months. The question is no longer whether AI can help researchers find vulnerabilities, but whether AI is changing vulnerability discovery faster than organizations are prepared to manage the risk.
Would your team catch the next zero-day in time?
Join security leaders who rely on the Think Newsletter for curated news on AI, cybersecurity, data and automation. Learn fast from expert tutorials and explainers—delivered directly to your inbox twice weekly. See the
IBM Privacy Statement
.
Thank you!
You are subscribed.
Key Takeaways:
Vulnerability disclosures are up 578% in 2026 across major software vendors.
Publicly disclosed CVEs across Microsoft, Oracle, Google Chrome and Apache increased from approximately 1,493 disclosures during January-September 2025 to more than 10,124 during the same period in 2026, representing roughly a 578% increase.
The acceleration became most apparent in Q2 2026.
Vulnerability disclosure volumes remained relatively stable through the first quarter before increasing sharply beginning in April and continuing through the summer months.
55% of AI-discovered vulnerabilities were high or critical, 91% remotely accessible.
X-Force analysis found that 55.2% of AI-attributed vulnerabilities were classified as High or Critical severity based on
NIST National Vulnerability Database (NVD) CVSS v3 ratings
, and that 91.0% were remotely accessible.
The challenge for defenders is shifting from discovery to prioritization.
As AI scales vulnerability discovery, keeping pace with remediation may become more difficult than finding vulnerabilities in the first place.
The implications extend well beyond vulnerability research teams. Historically, identifying vulnerabilities and exposed assets was often the limiting factor; increasingly, the challenge is determining which findings matter most and remediating them before attackers can exploit them. Organizations should therefore prepare for larger patch cycles, greater prioritization demands, compressed remediation timelines and mounting pressure on vulnerability management programs.
Vulnerability discovery appears to have entered a new phase
IBM X-Force observed a substantial increase in publicly disclosed Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) across multiple major software vendors throughout 2026. Across Microsoft, Oracle, Google Chrome and Apache, publicly disclosed CVEs rose from approximately 1,493 between January and September 2025 to more than 10,124 during the same period in 2026—an increase of roughly 578%. While disclosure activity naturally fluctuates over time, the magnitude of this increase warrants closer examination.
The timing of the growth is particularly notable. Vulnerability disclosure volumes remained relatively aligned with historical baselines through the first quarter of 2026 before beginning to accelerate in April. By the summer months, disclosure activity had reached levels significantly higher than those observed during the same period in 2025. Oracle, Microsoft, Google Chrome and Apache each experienced substantial increases, suggesting the trend was not limited to a single vendor, product category or software ecosystem. The increase also aligns with the growing availability and broader adoption of frontier AI models supporting vulnerability discovery among security researchers and organizations. While the available data does not establish a direct causal relationship, the timing and scale of the increase suggest AI-assisted research may be contributing to higher vulnerability disclosure volumes.
More importantly, the consistency of the pattern raises broader questions about how vulnerability research is evolving. Microsoft vulnerability disclosures increased by approximately 204% year-over-year, while Oracle, Google Chrome and Apache increased by approximately 1,292%, 2,456% and 367%, respectively. Such increases, from dozens of vulnerabilities per month to hundreds and, in some cases, thousands, suggest a meaningful change in how vulnerabilities are identified, validated, or reported, although the available data does not establish a single cause.
At the same time, recent research demonstrates that AI-assisted systems can identify vulnerabilities at unprecedented scale. The available data does not establish a direct causal relationship between AI-assisted research and increased disclosure activity. Taken together, however, these developments raise the possibility that vulnerability discovery is entering a new phase characterized by higher volumes and greater use of AI-assisted research.

AI is increasing the scale of vulnerability research
The vulnerability disclosure surge observed throughout 2026 coincides with broader advances in AI-assisted security research. While automation has supported vulnerability identification for years, recent developments suggest artificial intelligence is expanding the scale at which software can be analyzed for security weaknesses.
Research published by Unit 42 demonstrates how modern AI-assisted workflows can review source code, identify potential flaws, validate findings, generate proof-of-concepts and assist with remediation recommendations. This is all being completed at a pace difficult to achieve through traditional human-driven processes alone. If vulnerability discovery can increasingly operate at machine speed and machine scale, the growth in vulnerability disclosures observed by IBM X-Force throughout 2026 becomes considerably less surprising.
The emergence of autonomous vulnerability discovery systems alongside a dramatic increase in publicly disclosed vulnerabilities raises an important possibility: vulnerability research may be shifting from a process constrained by human bandwidth to one increasingly enabled by AI-assisted scale and automation.

The defender’s challenge has changed
The implications of AI-assisted vulnerability discovery extend beyond the number of vulnerabilities being reported. IBM X-Force analysis of 223 publicly reported vulnerabilities discovered using frontier AI models, among the most capable AI systems currently available. Of those vulnerabilities, 55.2% were classified as High or Critical severity based on NIST NVD CVSS v3 ratings, while 91.0% were remotely accessible, and 25.6% supported code execution. These findings suggest AI-assisted research is producing vulnerabilities that frequently require prioritization and remediation rather than simply surfacing a greater volume of low-risk findings.
The operational challenge is becoming more apparent, as vulnerability discovery accelerates. Security teams may be required to assess, prioritize and remediate a growing number of severe and remotely exploitable vulnerabilities within the same resource constraints and response windows. For many organizations, the limiting factor is no longer visibility into vulnerabilities, but the capacity to determine which findings present the greatest risk and respond accordingly.
At the same time, AI is reshaping the vulnerability landscape for both defenders and attackers. While defenders benefit from increased visibility into software weaknesses, adversaries gain access to the same growing volume of publicly disclosed vulnerabilities. As AI-assisted research continues to mature, organizations should expect larger patch cycles, greater triage demands, compressed remediation timelines and increasing pressure on vulnerability management programs.

What defenders should do next
Artificial intelligence is not only changing how vulnerabilities are discovered. It may be fundamentally changing the pace at which vulnerabilities are identified, disclosed and remediated. While the direct impact of AI-assisted research on vulnerability disclosures remains difficult to quantify, the dramatic increase observed throughout 2026 raises important questions about how vulnerability research is evolving.
As vulnerability discovery continues to scale, the challenge for defenders is no longer simply discovering vulnerabilities. It is determining which vulnerabilities matter most and responding before attackers do. Practical steps defenders can take now include:
Prioritize based on risk, not volume
.
Focus remediation efforts on vulnerabilities with the greatest exposure, exploitability and business impact.
Reduce remediation delays
.
Review patching and change management processes to ensure critical vulnerabilities can be addressed quickly.
Improve visibility into exposed systems
.
Maintain continuous awareness of internet-facing assets, applications and services.
Leverage compensating controls when needed.
Consider virtual patching and other mitigation measures when immediate remediation is not feasible.
Prepare for increasing disclosure volumes
.

items.title: Four CTEM Fails and How to Fix ThemRead More
items.content:
Four CTEM Fails and How to Fix Them
By:
Brian Moran, VP of Product Marketing
October 15, 2026
Long before Mythos, vulnerability management teams were already drowning in more vulnerabilities than any team could possibly manage with speed and scale.
Gartner analysts created continuous threat exposure management (CTEM) as a framework to reduce the “risk-to-fix” gap – or as a recent Gartner report plainly stated:
Your objective is to shift exposure management from counting vulnerabilities to measuring how quickly attacker-relevant exposures are identified, validated and mitigated within defined response objectives.
Gartner, Modernize Exposure Management to Counter AI-Augmented Vulnerability Discovery, Mitchell Schneider, Jonathan Nunez, September 24, 2026.
However, the old habits of vulnerability management are hard to break. Many security teams struggled to meet CTEM's new demands, ranging from exposure validation to workflows requiring collaboration across the security team.
Many security team CTEM challenges comes down to four common failures:
Too little validation
Too much dependence on patching
A program trapped inside vulnerability management
Collaboration that adds more handoffs than action
In the world of Mythos and AI-powered exposure discovery, weaponization and targeted campaigns, we must quickly learn from the CTEM 1.0 mistakes and evolve security programs to prove, prioritize and adapt at machine speed.
Here is how security teams can address each of these four failures.
CTEM fail #1: Validation without evidence of security control effectiveness
Going back to the early research on CTEM, Gartner focused on the need for validation to answer the critical question: how would our controls and response cope with an attack against the exposure?
i
However, many CTEM programs added theoretical validation by only considering what passive scanning can provide. For example, attack surface management (ASM) provides attack path mapping to understand how attackers could theoretically reach the exposure and the systems potentially accessed downstream of the exposure.
A theoretical attack path does not indicate whether an attacker can complete it within the organization’s environment. It does not prove whether an endpoint policy will stop execution, a network control will block movement or a security information and event management (SIEM) rule will generate an alert.
Security control configuration audits (often called automated security control assessments) provide another form of theoretical validation. The idea is that the configuration of the security control can validate which threats can and cannot be blocked or detected.
Like the theoretical attack paths of ASM, these control audits are essentially risk modeling without the proof and evidence of how the exposure can be exploited in your environment.
The fix: Make validation the central filter
Validation should separate discovered exposures from exposures that require immediate action.
Security teams should use automated attack simulation to safely reproduce the attacker behavior associated with an exposure. The test should measure whether controls prevent the attack, whether detection systems identify it and whether response processes produce the expected action.
This creates a practical set of outcomes:
Prevented and detected:
The current controls reduce immediate risk and provide response visibility
Prevented and not detected:
Prevention works, but the organization may lack evidence or warning of attempted exploitation
Not prevented and detected:
The attack can progress, but defenders have an opportunity to respond
Not prevented and not detected:
The exposure presents the highest urgency because the attack can succeed without an alert
Validation gives each team the same evidence. Vulnerability management can see exploitability. SecOps can see control performance. Security engineering can identify the failed policy or rule. Business and IT owners receive proof of why the issue requires action.
The outcome is focus: a broad set of potential exposures becomes an actionable list of gaps proven to matter in the organization’s environment.
CTEM fail #2: Patching is treated as the only response
Patching remains essential, but it rarely moves at the speed of exploitation.
A patch may require testing, a maintenance window, application owner approval and a rollback plan. Some systems cannot tolerate immediate downtime. Other exposures have no vendor patch available. Even an emergency process can leave a meaningful gap between disclosure and deployment.
A CTEM program that sends every validated exposure to the patch queue inherits the patch process' speed limits. The risk remains open while attackers continue to move.
This patch-first mindset can also miss faster ways to interrupt an attack. A control update may block the relevant technique in minutes or hours. A virtual patch may protect an exposed application while developers test the permanent fix. Segmentation, identity changes or service restrictions may remove the attacker’s path.
The fix: Mobilize through the fastest, most effective mitigation
The response should begin with one question: Which available action can reduce risk fastest?
Depending on the exposure, that action may include:
Blocking indicators of compromise across endpoint, email, network and cloud controls
Applying a web application firewall (WAF) rule or virtual patch
Updating an endpoint detection and response (EDR) prevention policy
Creating or tuning a SIEM, EDR or NDR detection rule
Disabling an unnecessary service or restricting access
Reducing identity privileges or revoking active sessions
Segmenting a vulnerable asset from untrusted systems
Deploying the permanent software patch
The team should test the proposed mitigation against the same attack used to validate the exposure. A successful retest proves that the control change reduced risk. Patching can then continue according to operational requirements without leaving the organization unprotected.
This approach does not weaken patching. It adds protection during the period when a permanent fix is unavailable or unsafe to deploy.
CTEM should track time to protection alongside time to patch. The first metric shows how quickly the organization reduced the immediate risk. The second shows what happens when the underlying flaw is removed.
CTEM fail #3: The program is vulnerability management with a new name
For many organizations, CTEM remains a slow evolution of vulnerability management. Teams added asset importance, business context, threat intelligence and attack-path data to improve prioritization.
That is useful progress. It does not create a complete CTEM program if the work remains within a single function.
Vulnerability management can discover and organize exposures. It usually does not own threat analysis, offensive testing, security control configuration, incident detection or production patch deployment. If the program stops with a prioritized list, the teams responsible for reducing risk still receive another queue of work.
This model also narrows the definition of exposure. Security gaps include vulnerable software, but they also include misconfigurations, excessive privileges, exposed services, missing detections and ineffective controls. A program centered on CVEs can overlook these paths.
The fix: Build CTEM as a program-wide operating model
CTEM needs defined roles across the security and IT organization:
Vulnerability management
discovers exposures and maps them to affected assets
Cyber threat intelligence
explains relevant attacker behavior and active campaigns
Red teams and validation teams
prove which exposures can be exploited
SecOps and blue teams
improve prevention, detection and response
Security engineering
changes control configurations and builds durable protections
IT and application owners
patch systems and make production changes
These teams should align on a shared outcome: reducing the business risk associated with validated exposure.
That requires common measures. A program-wide CTEM dashboard should show more than vulnerability counts and remediation age. It should track validated gaps, control failures, mitigation status, time to protection and confirmation that each fix worked.
Governance matters as well. Leaders should define which team owns each stage, how urgent findings are escalated and who can approve compensating controls. Clear ownership prevents validated exposures from sitting between teams.
CTEM fail #4: Collaboration creates slow, manual handoffs
Moving CTEM beyond vulnerability management introduces a new problem. More teams become involved, but they work in different systems with different priorities and processes.
A typical exposure may pass from a scanner to vulnerability management, then to threat intelligence for research, to a red team for testing, to SecOps for control analysis and to IT for remediation. Each handoff requires someone to interpret the previous team’s work, create a ticket and wait for the next available specialist.
The program becomes collaborative on paper while the actual response remains fragmented. Delays accumulate between discovery, validation and mitigation.
AI-powered threats make those delays more costly. A process measured in days cannot reliably respond to an attack that unfolds in hours.
The fix: Automate the workflow from discovery through retesting
The first step is to identify repeatable handoffs and turn them into automated triggers.
A newly discovered exposure can trigger the collection of threat intelligence and asset context. The workflow can map the exposure to a relevant attack scenario, launch a safe validation test and deliver the evidence to the teams responsible for action. A failed control can trigger a mitigation workflow. Once the approved change is deployed, the system can rerun the test and record the result.
Agentic AI can support tasks that previously required an analyst at each step. An agent can summarize the threat, map it to the environment, prepare a tailored assessment and recommend the security controls positioned to interrupt the attack. People review evidence and approve sensitive changes while the routine handles research, coordination and repeatable execution.
Effective automation should connect the existing systems used by each team. The goal is a continuous flow of context and evidence, not another console that requires manual monitoring.
A practical automated CTEM workflow looks like this:
Discover an exposure and identify affected assets
Enrich it with threat, business and control context
Build and run a relevant attack simulation
Prioritize the exposure using observed impact
Recommend the fastest and most effective mitigation
Route the action to the correct owner
Deploy the approved change
Retest and record proof of risk reduction
This sequence shortens the time between identifying a problem and proving that the organization has fixed it.
Move CTEM from ranked findings to validated outcomes
The first generation of CTEM improved how organizations manage exposure data. The next step is to improve how quickly they reduce risk.
That requires four changes:
Replace theoretical prioritization with offensive validation
Expand the response beyond patching to include mitigation, virtual patching and control optimization
Operate CTEM across vulnerability management, threat intelligence, offensive security, SecOps, engineering and IT
Automate the handoffs that delay validation and action
Together, these changes create a continuous cycle: discover, validate, mitigate and retest. Teams gain evidence about which exposures matter, which controls failed and which actions worked.
AI is increasing the speed and volume of threats. CTEM must give defenders the same advantage. Success should be measured by how fast the organization can prove risk, reduce it and adapt its defenses before the next attack.

As we navigate through 2026, the cybersecurity landscape has become more complex than ever. Ransomware has evolved from simple encryption scripts into highly sophisticated, AI-driven operations that target organizations of all sizes. Cybercriminals now leverage advanced automation, deepfakes, and triple-extortion tactics to maximize their impact. Staying ahead of these threats requires more than just basic antivirus software; it demands a comprehensive, proactive approach to digital security and data resilience. Today, a single breach can cripple global supply chains, paralyze critical infrastructure, and cause devastating financial and reputational ruin within hours. Security is no longer solely an IT department problem; it is a fundamental business imperative. Leaders must foster a culture of vigilance, continuously adapting their defenses to outsmart relentless digital adversaries.
Learning Objectives
By reading this article, you will be able to:
Understand
the core mechanics of a modern ransomware attack.
Identify
the different types and tactics used by cybercriminals in 2026.
Execute
an immediate incident response plan if your system is compromised.
Implement
robust, future-proof strategies to defend your data and infrastructure against future attacks.
What is a Ransomware Attack?
A ransomware attack is a highly disruptive form of malicious software (malware) deployment designed to block access to a computer system, network, or critical data until a sum of money—the ransom—is paid to the perpetrators. Attackers achieve this hostile takeover by utilizing advanced cryptographic algorithms to encrypt the victim’s files, rendering them completely unusable and inaccessible without a specific, attacker-controlled decryption key. What once began as opportunistic attacks on individual consumers has now transformed into a massive, organized criminal enterprise targeting corporations, hospitals, and government agencies. In recent years, the anatomy of these attacks has grown increasingly vicious. Beyond merely locking systems, modern threat actors now routinely exfiltrate (steal) vast amounts of sensitive data before triggering the encryption process. This tactic is leveraged to threaten victims with the public release of confidential client records, trade secrets, or embarrassing internal communications if their demands are ignored. Consequently, even organizations with perfect data backups are forced into a corner, as they must protect their reputation and avoid massive regulatory fines associated with data breaches. The deployment of ransomware often relies on exploiting human vulnerabilities or technical loopholes. Once inside a network, the malware stealthily moves laterally, seeking out vital servers and disabling security software before making its presence known. The resulting operational paralysis can bring business activities to a grinding halt, causing millions of dollars in downtime, lost revenue, and recovery costs, making it one of the most feared cyber threats of the modern era.
Key elements of a modern ransomware deployment include:
Initial Compromise:
The breach usually begins through deceptive phishing emails, stolen credentials, or unpatched software vulnerabilities.
Lateral Movement:
Attackers quietly navigate the compromised network to locate the most valuable data and disable backup systems.
Encryption and Extortion:
Files are locked with military-grade encryption, accompanied by a digital ransom note demanding payment, typically in cryptocurrency.
Data Exfiltration:
Sensitive information is secretly transferred to attacker-controlled servers to serve as leverage for secondary blackmail.
What Are the Types of Ransomware Attacks?
The landscape of ransomware is no longer defined by a single, predictable method of attack. Over the past decade, cybercriminals have heavily diversified their arsenals, transforming ransomware into a complex ecosystem of specialized threats designed to exploit different vulnerabilities. Attackers now carefully tailor their approaches based on their target’s industry, size, and specific security posture, moving far beyond the rudimentary “encrypt and demand” tactics of the early 2000s to maximize their leverage and payout potential. A major driver of this diversification is the rapid industrialization of cybercrime. The underground economy has matured into a highly structured environment, leading to sophisticated business models where malware development, initial network access, and attack execution are handled by entirely different criminal syndicates. This professionalization means that highly advanced, weaponized code is now accessible even to novice attackers, exponentially increasing the sheer volume, variety, and geographic spread of attacks that organizations face on a daily basis. In 2026, the most alarming shift is the integration of artificial intelligence and the aggressive expansion of the victim pool. Autonomous malware can now analyze network defenses in real-time and adapt its behavior to remain undetected, while ruthless extortion strategies have escalated to involve not just the breached company, but its entire supply chain and customer base. Understanding these distinct threat categories is the first crucial step in building a resilient, targeted defense strategy.
The primary categories of ransomware operating today include:
Crypto and Locker Variants:
The foundational forms of the threat. Crypto-ransomware selectively encrypts critical business files and databases while leaving the basic operating system running to display the ransom note. Locker ransomware, conversely, completely freezes the user out of the device’s interface, rendering the entire machine completely inaccessible.
Double & Triple Extortion:
A ruthless escalation tactic. Attackers first steal massive amounts of sensitive data before encrypting the local copies, threatening to leak the information on the dark web if unpaid (double extortion). In triple extortion campaigns, attackers actively harass and demand ransoms directly from the breached organization’s clients, business partners, or employees.
Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS):
A highly profitable franchising model for cybercrime. Elite developers create sophisticated ransomware variants and lease them out to “affiliates” on the dark web. The affiliates handle the actual hacking and deployment, and both parties split the resulting ransom profits, vastly lowering the barrier to entry for cybercrime.
AI-Automated Ransomware:
The latest and most advanced evolution in threat vectors. These autonomous, intelligent malware strains leverage machine learning to actively evade endpoint detection systems, identify the most critical data silos to target, and execute the encryption payload at speeds human defenders simply cannot manually counter.
What Should I Do If I Am Attacked?
Discovering that your systems have been compromised by ransomware is a high-stress scenario, but how you react in the first few minutes can dictate the entire outcome of the crisis. Panic and rash decisions often exacerbate the damage, allowing the malware to spread further or destroying crucial digital evidence. A calm, structured, and immediate response is absolutely critical to containing the blast radius and preventing a localized infection from turning into a catastrophic, company-wide blackout. The immediate aftermath of an attack is not the time for improvisation; it requires strict adherence to a pre-established incident response plan. Many victims make the fatal mistake of acting on instinct—such as rebooting infected servers in hopes of clearing the glitch, or immediately reaching out to the attackers to negotiate. These knee-jerk reactions almost always work in favor of the cybercriminals. Rebooting can trigger aggressive secondary encryption routines or wipe the volatile system memory that forensic experts desperately need to trace the attackers’ steps and identify the specific malware variant. Once the initial containment is achieved, the focus must shift to professional triage and secure recovery. Engaging specialized incident response teams, legal counsel, and law enforcement ensures that you are handling the extortion demands and data breach notifications in compliance with 2026’s strict regulatory frameworks. Recovery is a meticulous process of finding the initial entry point, eliminating the backdoor, and carefully rebuilding the environment so that the attackers cannot simply strike again the moment you bring your systems back online.
If you suspect an active ransomware infection, immediately follow these four critical steps:
Isolate the Infection Immediately:
Time is your most valuable asset. Instantly disconnect all affected devices and servers from the corporate network, Wi-Fi, internet, and any shared cloud storage to physically halt the malware from moving laterally to other systems.
Avoid Destructive Knee-Jerk Reactions:
Do not reboot or shut down the compromised machines, as this can accelerate encryption or destroy vital forensic evidence stored in the RAM. Furthermore, do not immediately pay the ransom; paying rarely guarantees full data recovery and instantly marks your organization as a lucrative, compliant target for future attacks.
Engage Experts and Notify Authorities:
Alert your internal security operations center (SOC) or external incident response providers immediately. Simultaneously, report the breach to relevant cyber law enforcement agencies, who may already have decryption keys for specific RaaS variants or intelligence on the threat actors.
Assess, Clean, and Restore Safely:
Work with forensics to identify exactly what data was compromised and how the attackers gained entry. Only after completely patching the vulnerabilities and purging the network of hidden backdoors should you begin restoring your systems from secure, immutable backups.
Effective Ransomware Protection Strategies for 2026
As ransomware tactics have evolved into multi-layered extortion campaigns driven by rapid automation, traditional perimeter-based security is no longer sufficient to protect an organization in 2026. The days of relying solely on basic antivirus software and standard firewalls are completely obsolete against modern adversaries who utilize artificial intelligence to bypass legacy systems. Today, defending a corporate network or personal infrastructure requires a proactive, dynamic approach that actively anticipates breaches rather than merely reacting to them after the damage is done. To effectively counter these sophisticated threats, organizations must transition to a comprehensive “defense-in-depth” methodology. This strategy operates on the realistic assumption that a network will eventually be breached, placing a heavy emphasis on containing the threat, severely restricting the malware’s lateral movement, and ensuring rapid, guaranteed recovery capabilities. It is about building an incredibly resilient environment where a single compromised credential or one vulnerable endpoint does not automatically result in a catastrophic, company-wide encryption event. Furthermore, true cyber resilience in 2026 seamlessly blends cutting-edge technological safeguards with a highly trained workforce. While autonomous AI defenses hunt for anomalous behavior at machine speed, human employees must serve as an alert and educated frontline against increasingly deceptive social engineering and deepfake attacks. By aligning advanced architecture with continuous operational vigilance, businesses can create an overwhelmingly hostile environment for cybercriminals, drastically reducing the likelihood of a successful extortion attempt.
To defend against the sophisticated threats of 2026, organizations and individuals must adopt these critical security measures:
Immutable Backups:
Maintain specialized backups that cannot be altered, deleted, or encrypted by anyone—even by individuals possessing top-level administrative privileges. Ensure these critical data reserves are stored entirely offline or in a highly secure, logically isolated cloud vault.
Zero Trust Architecture:
Adopt a strict “never trust, always verify” approach across the entire digital infrastructure. Continuously authenticate users and limit access to only the specific data and systems absolutely necessary for their immediate role (the Least Privilege Principle).
AI-Powered Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR):
Utilize next-generation security platforms that rely on continuous behavioral analysis and machine learning, rather than outdated signature matching, to identify and automatically terminate ransomware before it can execute its encryption payload.
Phishing-Resistant MFA:
Enforce Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) universally across all internal and external accounts. In 2026, organizations must pivot away from easily intercepted SMS codes and rely on physical hardware security keys (like FIDO2) or secure biometrics.
Continuous Security Awareness Training:
Human error remains the most exploited vulnerability in any network. Regularly and rigorously train employees to recognize AI-generated deepfakes, highly personalized spear-phishing emails, and the latest social engineering tactics designed to steal credentials.
Conclusion
Ransomware in 2026 has undeniably cemented itself as a formidable and relentless adversary, characterized by lightning-fast execution speeds and ruthlessly complex, multi-layered extortion tactics. The days of isolated, easily mitigated ransomware strains are long gone, replaced by highly orchestrated campaigns driven by artificial intelligence and sophisticated criminal syndicates. These modern attacks do not merely seek to temporarily disrupt operations; they aim to fundamentally paralyze entire organizations, compromise highly sensitive intellectual property, and extort maximum financial payouts by weaponizing both encrypted systems and stolen data simultaneously. However, despite the escalating sophistication of these threat actors, a catastrophic and successful attack is by no means inevitable. By deeply understanding the evolving nature of these digital threats and establishing exactly how to respond with clinical precision during a crisis, organizations can drastically minimize their exposure. The key to survival lies in shifting from a reactive mindset to a highly proactive one, implementing resilient, modern defense frameworks that anticipate failure. By embedding robust strategies such as truly immutable backups, stringent Zero Trust architectures, and AI-driven endpoint detection into the core of their operations, businesses can neutralize an attack long before the ransom note ever appears on a screen. Ultimately, achieving absolute security in an increasingly hyper-connected world is an illusion, but achieving profound resilience is an entirely realistic goal. Cybersecurity must be viewed not as a static destination or a simple checklist of software purchases, but rather as a continuous, dynamic journey of adaptation and improvement. As cybercriminals inevitably develop new tools and tactics to bypass contemporary defenses, organizations must remain equally committed to evolving their strategies and empowering their human workforce through relentless education. By staying comprehensively informed, culturally vigilant, and technologically prepared, you forge your strongest possible shield against the ransomware threats of tomorrow.
